summary: Specifies an RTP payload format for carrying the ETSI ES 201 108 front-end feature streams used in distributed speech recognition. In such systems the device processes speech and a remote server finishes recognition. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A phone can do the first part of understanding speech and send a compact summary to a faster computer. This memo says how to pack that summary for the internet.

questions: how big is an es 201 108 frame pair
subtitle: How to pack the compact speech features a phone computes into RTP packets so a remote server can recognize the words.

tldr.problem: Voice codecs on mobile devices are built for audible quality, not for speech recognition accuracy, and the network damages the signal further before a server-side recognizer sees it.
tldr.mechanism: The device runs the ETSI ES 201 108 front end itself and sends the resulting features in 12-octet frame pairs, each covering 20 ms of speech, inside ordinary RTP packets.
tldr.outcome: Clients and speech engines from different makers get one common packet format, with the number of frame pairs per packet traded off between bandwidth efficiency and delay.

today: RFC 3557 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself says it expects many VoIP and mobile applications to use the media type.

sections.title: Why Distributed Speech Recognition
sections.content:
Voice interfaces to services such as airline information systems and unified messaging are becoming more common, and so are mobile devices. The problem is that the voice codecs in mobile devices were designed for audible voice quality and not for speech recognition accuracy. Channel errors and lost packets degrade the signal further.

In a traditional system the whole recognizer sits on the server and must work with whatever arrives after the network decodes the vocoded speech. In a distributed speech recognition (DSR) system the remote device is a thin client, the front end. It processes the speech, compresses the data and adds error protection suited to recognition. The speech engine then uses that representation directly.

The ETSI Aurora working group published such a format as standard ES 201 108 in February 2000. RFC 3550's RTP is a good fit because voice dialogues need low latency, so this memo defines how to carry the ES 201 108 data in RTP.
sections.eli5: Sending whole sound recordings over a bad connection can garble them. So the phone does the first part of the listening itself and sends only the useful notes, which survive the trip better.

sections.title: The ES 201 108 Front End and Where It Is Used
sections.content:
ES 201 108 defines a signal processing front end and compression scheme. It uses a standard mel-cepstral technique, supports raw sampling rates of 8 kHz, 11 kHz and 16 kHz, and produces an output vector every 10 ms. The vectors are quantized with split-vector quantization to cut the data rate, and the quantized vectors from two consecutive frames are put into a frame pair (FP).

The memo shows three scenarios: an IP user terminal talking directly to an IP speech engine, a non-IP terminal reaching an IP speech engine through a gateway, and an IP terminal reaching a non-IP speech engine through a gateway. In all of them the recognizer lives in the speech engine, and the encoder in the user terminal sends frame pairs. Each FP holds two sets of encoded vectors representing 20 ms of original speech.
sections.eli5: The phone chops your voice into tiny slices and writes a short note about each one. Two notes in a row make one pair, and each pair covers a very short moment of talking.

sections.title: The RTP Payload
sections.content:
A DSR RTP packet is a standard RTP header from RFC 3550 followed by a payload made by concatenating a series of FPs. FPs are packed bit-contiguously from the most significant bit. Each FP is 96 bits, or 12 octets, so the payload always ends on an octet boundary.

The memo's example shows a packet carrying three 96-bit FPs one after another after the RTP header.
sections.eli5: Each packet is an envelope with a standard label on the outside and a stack of identical-size note pairs inside. Because every pair is the same size, the stack always fits neatly.

sections.title: Packet Size and Silence Handling
sections.content:
The number of FPs per packet should follow the application's latency and bandwidth needs. Fewer FPs per packet lowers bandwidth efficiency because of RTP/UDP/IP header overhead. More FPs per packet means longer end-to-end delay and more recognition latency, and it raises the chance of a catastrophic loss of many consecutive FPs, which most recognizers handle badly. The memo therefore RECOMMENDS keeping the number of FPs per packet as small as the bandwidth requirements allow, and suggests considering header compression such as RFC 2508 and RFC 3095.

The payload may also support discontinuous transmission (DTX), where FPs are sent only when speech is detected. A run of frames for an unbroken speech segment is a transmission segment. It ends when consecutive non-speech frames exceed a threshold called the hangover time; the memo gives 1.5 seconds as a typical value. After the last FP the front end SHOULD send one or more Null FPs to mark the end.
sections.eli5: Putting many note pairs in one envelope saves stamps but makes you wait longer, and losing one envelope hurts more. When you stop talking, the phone stops sending and then sends a special empty note to say it is done.

sections.title: Frame Pair Formats
sections.content:
Each mel-cepstral frame is 44 bits and represents 10 ms of voice. Pairs of quantized frames MUST be grouped and protected with a 4-bit CRC, forming a 92-bit FP. Each FP MUST then be padded with 4 zero bits to reach a 32-bit word boundary, which makes it 96 bits. This padding is separate from the padding indicated by the P bit in the RTP header. The CRC MUST be computed with the formula in section 6.2.4 of ES 201 108, which also defines the indices and how their values are found.

A Null FP marks the end of a transmission segment. Both frames are set to null, meaning the first 88 bits are filled with zeros. The CRC is calculated the same way and 4 zeros MUST be padded on the end.
sections.eli5: Each pair is two short notes, a small check code to spot damage, and a few blank bits at the end so everything lines up. The empty note is all blanks plus its check code.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
The RTP timestamp is the sampling instant of the first sample encoded for the first FP in the packet. The clock frequency equals the sampling frequency, so the timestamp counts samples. One FP lasts 20 ms, which is 160, 220 or 320 samples at 8, 11 or 16 kHz, so the timestamp rises by 160, 220 or 320 per consecutive FP.

The payload is always a whole number of octets. If padding is needed for another reason, the RTP P bit may be set and padding appended as RFC 3550 describes. The marker bit should follow the general rules in RFC 3551. The memo does not assign an RTP payload type; it expects the RTP profile to assign one or to bind it dynamically.
sections.eli5: Every packet carries a time stamp that counts how far into the recording it starts. The count goes up by the same amount for each note pair.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Mapping
sections.content:
The memo registers one new MIME subtype: media type audio, subtype dsr-es201108, with no required parameters. The optional rate parameter gives the sample rate with valid values 8000, 11000 and 16000, and 8000 is assumed if it is absent. The optional maxptime is the maximum media per packet in milliseconds, SHOULD be a multiple of the FP duration of 20 ms, and defaults to 80 ms. If a high packet loss ratio is expected, a shorter value MAY be chosen.

In SDP, the media type goes in the m= line, the subtype in a=rtpmap as the encoding name, rate as the clock rate in the same line, and ptime and maxptime in the attributes of the same names.
sections.eli5: This section gives the format an official name and a few settings, like how often to send and how fast the sound was sampled, so two devices can agree before they start.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Implementations are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification, RFC 3550, and the RTP profile, RFC 3551. The payload format does not specify any different security services.
sections.eli5: This memo adds no new locks. It relies on the protections that RTP already has.

fields.name: Frame #1
fields.desc: Quantized mel-cepstral frame for 10 ms of voice.

fields.name: Frame #2
fields.desc: Next quantized frame, 10 ms of voice.

fields.name: CRC
fields.desc: 4-bit CRC calculated as in section 6.2.4 of ES 201 108.

fields.name: Padding
fields.desc: Four zero bits for 32-bit word alignment.
